meta.tagline: Brick streets where revolution was born, chowder steam and wicked pride

overview.title: Welcome to Boston
overview.intro: Boston is America's most European city: brick sidewalks, gaslit streets and university rowers pulling along the river. Revolution fermented here — the red line of the Freedom Trail tells the whole story in four kilometers, from tea party to first shot. Across the river, Harvard and MIT run the world's brain center; the North End's Italian bakeries smell of cannoli, and oyster shells clink along the harbor. A Bostonian is 'wicked' proud of the accent, the teams and the city — give it a few days and you will be too.

local_word.definition: In Boston English it means 'very': 'wicked good', 'wicked smaht'. Nothing to do with evil — it adds emphasis and pride. Once a Bostonian declares the chowder 'wicked good', the debate is over. Use the word in the right place and the city takes you in.

rules.title: Walk the Freedom Trail on your own feet
rules.description: The red brick line in the pavement links all 16 stops by itself: you don't even need a map. You're not obliged to pay for tours — follow the line; most stops are free. Start early: the Faneuil area gets crowded by noon.

rules.title: Befriend the T, forget the car
rules.description: America's oldest subway covers the city well enough; a car in Boston means narrow one-ways, aggressive drivers and a legendary parking problem. Get a CharlieCard, learn the green and red lines — the city is walkable anyway.

rules.title: Visit both banks of the river
rules.description: Boston is not only Boston: across the Charles lies Cambridge — Harvard's yards, MIT's corridors and the bookshops. Give the far bank half a day; the Esplanade riverside walk home is the city's loveliest 'bridge'.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: ~15 min to town — even a water taxi

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: The Rs go missing: 'pahk the cah'

tip.label: The Boston philosophy
tip.text: This city is lived on foot and by season: autumn leaves, spring rowing, summer harbor. Don't overpack the program — Boston's best moments arrive on their own, on a harbor bench, in a college yard, or on a dive bar stool.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Boston is compact and walkable; the T fills the gaps and ferries open the harbor — you don't need a car, and a car is in fact a burden.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: Logan sits at the city's edge: the Blue Line + Silver Line combination reaches the center in half an hour, and the water taxi entrance through the harbor is the most stylish hello. Taxis are quick but subject to tunnel traffic.

items.title: The T
items.description: America's first subway, running since 1897: colored lines, boarded with a CharlieCard. The Green Line crawls like a tram but charms; the Red Line reaches Harvard. It closes early — check the last train.

items.title: A walkable city
items.description: Boston is America's most walkable city: Beacon Hill to the North End, the Common to the harbor, everything within steps. Brick sidewalks dislike heels — comfortable shoes are the Freedom Trail's official equipment.

items.title: Ferries and the harbor
items.description: The Charlestown ferry glides from Long Wharf to the USS Constitution in ten minutes: a harbor tour at commuter fare. In summer, ferries run to the Harbor Islands (Spectacle, Georges) — the city's least-known escape.

items.title: Bluebikes and the Esplanade
items.description: Bike share stations stand on every corner: the Esplanade and Memorial Drive routes are flat and scenic. On Sundays part of the riverside road closes to cars — the golden hour for pedaling.

callout.label: Harbor tip
callout.text: On a sunny afternoon board the Charlestown ferry at Long Wharf: skyline, gliding sailboats and the USS Constitution in one ride. Walk back through the North End and join the cannoli queue — Boston's two most efficient hours.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Boston the choice is a choice of atmosphere: Beacon Hill's gas lamps, the North End's bakery scent, Cambridge's campus rhythm.

local_word.definition: The three-story wooden Boston house, one flat per floor: a century-old architectural legacy of working-class immigration. From Dorchester to Somerville the neighborhoods are knit from these houses — their porched facades are the city's everyday face. Even if you don't stay in one, learn to spot it: this is the street fabric that makes Boston Boston.

items.name: Back Bay
items.description: Brownstone terraces, Newbury Street shopping and Copley Square: Boston's most photogenic quarter. Everything within a walk — the classic, polished base for a first visit.

items.name: Beacon Hill
items.description: The gaslit, cobblestoned hill quarter: Acorn Street's postcard frame lives here. Boutique hotels are few and precious — for waking up inside the historic atmosphere.

items.name: North End
items.description: Narrow streets, bakeries and pastry shops: America's oldest Italian quarter. Lively at night, espresso-scented in the morning — the address for a table-first stay.

items.name: Cambridge
items.description: Harvard Square's bookshops, cafes and buskers: the intellectual air of the far bank. Fifteen minutes to the center on the Red Line — prices a notch kinder.

items.name: Seaport
items.description: The new district of glass towers, seafood restaurants and museums: the Harborwalk at your doorstep. For modern hotel seekers — a walk or short ride to the center.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Boston is a city of seasons: an autumn leaf festival, spring graduation and rowing, summer harbor life, a winter harsh but heartfelt.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Oars and Magnolias
items.subtitle: Spring · Rowers on the river, blossoming brownstones
items.description: April magnolias dress the Back Bay facades, the Charles fills with rowing crews, and Marathon Monday turns the city into a festival. The weather is fickle but the energy high — hotels fill in graduation weeks.

callout.label: Marathon note
callout.text: On Patriots' Day in mid-April the Boston Marathon takes the city: roads close and hotels sell out months ahead. To watch, set up on Beacon Street; to avoid it, skip that weekend.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Harbor Season
items.subtitle: Summer · Warm evenings, island ferries, open-air concerts
items.description: Summer Boston moves to the harbor: island ferries, oyster-bar terraces and the Esplanade's open-air concerts. Humidity presses now and then, but the sea breeze arrives in time — the city's most social season.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: On July 4th the Boston Pops concert and fireworks on the Esplanade rank among America's most famous celebrations: claiming a spot is morning work. The calm alternative: watch the fireworks from the Cambridge bank.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: New England Leaf Festival
items.subtitle: Autumn · Crimson campuses, crystal skies
items.description: October is Boston's crown: the Common and the campuses turn crimson, the air runs clear and walker-friendly. The Head of the Charles regatta turns the river into a festival — New England fall is a feast even inside the city.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: On the mid-October Head of the Charles weekend, go down to the river: watch the world's largest regatta from the bridges. For a leaf tour, give a morning to the Arnold Arboretum — a forest festival inside the city.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Nor'easters and Hot Chowder
items.subtitle: Winter · Snowy brownstones, fogged pub windows
items.description: Boston winter is serious: nor'easter storms bring snow and the wind cuts deep. The rewards are postcard Beacon Hill, empty museums and chowder in steamy pubs. The city works through winter — layer up and work with it.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: On the morning after snowfall, go to Acorn Street: gas lamps, snowy cobbles and brick facades — Boston's most famous frame is at its best in this state. A hot bowl of clam chowder thaws frozen hands.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Boston table is a partnership of sea and migration: chowder steam, lobster rolls, Italian bakeries and the Dunkin cup — all civic identity.

local_word.definition: Clam chowder in the Boston accent: creamy, packed with clams, served with oyster crackers — the New England classic. Don't mention the red (Manhattan) version in Boston — here chowder is white, thick and a national matter.

items.name: New England clam chowder
items.description: Cream, clams and potato: the absolute answer to a cold day. In a bread bowl or a classic cup — crumble the oyster crackers on top and skip the debate: the white one is the real one.
items.tag: The national bowl · with oyster crackers

items.name: Lobster roll
items.description: Lobster in a buttered, toasted roll: cold with mayo (Maine style) or warm with butter (Connecticut style). Beside the harbor with fries — the price is serious, the happiness guaranteed.

items.name: The North End cannoli duel
items.description: Mike's or Modern: the city's sweetest feud. Crisp shell, ricotta filling and a queue — try both bakeries and choose your side. Espresso alongside is the Italian quarter's etiquette.

items.name: The oyster bar ritual
items.description: Wellfleet and Island Creek oysters on ice with mignonette: Boston's centuries-old oyster bars are among America's oldest. At happy hour the counter prices turn friendly.

items.name: The Dunkin ritual
items.description: In Boston, Dunkin is not a chain but an identity: a shop on every corner, an iced coffee in every hand — even in winter. Order it 'regulah' and it comes with cream and sugar; this is the cheapest way to blend in.
items.tag: Civic identity · iced even in winter

items.name: Boston cream pie
items.description: The cake that calls itself a pie: vanilla custard layers under chocolate glaze — the official dessert bearing the city's name. The version at its birthplace hotel is a pilgrimage; bakery versions are the daily reward.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: The Faneuil–Quincy Market zone serves mediocrity at tourist prices: leave the chowder and lobster to the storied harborside bars, the pastry to the North End bakeries. Tip 18–20% — wherever you sit down, it applies.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone walks the Freedom Trail; these six are Boston's book-scented, sea-breezed hidden pages.

items.rarity: The world inside a glass globe
items.name: The Mapparium
items.description: You walk through the inside of a three-story stained-glass globe from 1935: standing on the glass bridge you study the borders of 1935, while the acoustics carry a whisper to the far shore. Boston's strangest, most unforgettable half hour.

items.rarity: A fortress with a city beach
items.name: Castle Island
items.description: A fort and shoreline reached on foot in South Boston: the lawns of Fort Independence, planes on approach, and a hot dog from the Sullivan's stand. The locals' weekend classic — often missing from tourist maps.

items.name: SoWa Open Market
items.description: On Sundays the South End's old warehouse district opens with artist stalls, food trucks and a vintage market — and the gallery floors are open too. Boston's most pleasant Sunday ritual.

items.name: The Arnold Arboretum
items.description: Harvard's 281-acre tree collection: the jewel of the Emerald Necklace park chain. Leaves in October, lilacs in May — entry free, crowds far away.

items.rarity: The famous frame at its quietest
items.name: Acorn Street at dawn
items.description: America's most photographed street queues at midday and stands empty at 07:00: the cobbles, gas lamps and geraniums are yours. Pair it with Beacon Hill's side lanes.

items.name: The Harborwalk
items.description: The walking path wrapping the harbor: piers, parks and skyline views from the Seaport to the North End. The Fan Pier stretch at sunset — the city's best walk nobody talks about.

callout.label: Quiet hour strategy
callout.text: Boston's refinement opens early: Acorn Street at 07:00, the Freedom Trail at 08:00, Harvard Yard during class hours. The crowds arrive toward noon — take the morning for yourself and give midday to museums and the table.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Boston is an honest city; its traps hide in the shadow of historic titles — know these four.

items.name: The 'Cheers' bar letdown
items.description: The bar that 'inspired' the show offers a tourist queue, a souvenir counter and an ordinary menu: the interior isn't even the TV set.
items.instead: Take the photo outside and drink your beer in Beacon Hill's real neighborhood pubs. Boston's true 'everybody knows your name' bars are the storied dive bars on the corner.

items.name: Lobster prices at Quincy Market
items.description: The tourist market stalls sell a small lobster roll at peak price; you eat standing in a crowd and the flavor is average.
items.instead: Walk a few blocks: the storied harborside oyster bars and Seaport restaurants serve serious lobster for the same money. Tour Quincy Market for its building, not your dinner.

items.name: Renting a car in Boston
items.description: Narrow one-way streets, an aggressive driving culture and $40–60-a-day parking: in Boston a car is a burden, not freedom.
items.instead: The T + walking + ferries cover the city completely; rent a car only for the day of a New England excursion. The 'pahk the cah' joke is grounded in fact — there is no parking.

items.name: The Harvard tour hustlers
items.description: Around Harvard Square some 'official campus tour' sellers ticket you for yards that are free to roam; the storytelling is thin, the route short.
items.instead: The campus yards are open to the public: walk them yourself and smile at the 'three lies' of the John Harvard statue. The student-run free/tip-based tours tell the most entertaining version.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Boston, history is free: the Freedom Trail's line, the campus yards and the Harborwalk cost nothing. Save the budget for chowder, oysters and a Fenway ticket — the brick sidewalks tell the rest for free.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the red line to the cannoli queue

steps.title: Beacon Hill and Acorn Street
steps.description: A morning walk in the gaslit streets: shoot Acorn Street while it's still empty, then descend to the Common.

steps.title: Freedom Trail — first half
steps.description: Start at the Common: the State House, the burying grounds, the Old State House and the massacre site. The red line is your guide.

steps.title: Chowder break
steps.description: Clam chowder with oyster crackers by the harbor: in a bread bowl if it's cold. Don't forget to say 'wicked good'.

steps.title: North End and Old North Church
steps.description: Through the Italian quarter's narrow lanes onto Paul Revere's route: the church of the two lanterns and the historic house.

steps.title: Ferry to Charlestown
steps.description: From Long Wharf by boat to the USS Constitution: the world's oldest floating warship and the Bunker Hill obelisk.

steps.title: Cannoli and a pub finale
steps.description: Return to the North End: pick your side in the cannoli duel, then close the evening with a local beer in a storied pub.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Revolution, campus and harbor — the full Boston

steps.title: Classic Boston
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Beacon Hill, the Freedom Trail, chowder, the North End, Charlestown, a cannoli night.

steps.title: Cambridge and the river
steps.description: Red Line to Harvard in the morning: yards, bookshops and a square coffee; MIT's campus and museum at noon; an Esplanade walk or a Bluebikes river loop in the afternoon; a Newbury Street dinner in Back Bay.

steps.title: Art, park and Fenway
steps.description: The Isabella Stewart Gardner or the MFA in the morning; SoWa (if Sunday) or the Arnold Arboretum at noon; a Fenway Park tour in the afternoon — bleacher seats if there's a game; farewell happy hour oysters + a lobster roll.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: The Boston accent swallows its Rs but its heart is wide; these five phrases warm the city to you wicked fast.

items.meaning: Very — say 'wicked good' and the Bostonian smiles; the city's official adverb
The subway's name — 'take the T' is the city's transport sentence
The local name for Dunkin — a 'Dunks run' is the official declaration of a coffee break
The accent's legendary 'park the car' — make the joke before a local does
The Red Sox cheer — say it near Fenway and make instant friends

checklist.title: Boston Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Wicked good! You've lived the city of revolution the way it deserves!
